analysis.one_liner: Makes oil and gas drillers on federal leases replace damaged water supplies, compensate landowners, and reclaim drilled land.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the House Natural Resources Committee and its energy subcommittee until the Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: When companies drill for federally owned oil and gas on land the government sold the surface of, the landowner often gets no say and no compensation, and drilling — especially coalbed methane — can contaminate or drain the water wells and streams that farms and homes depend on. This bill would have required drillers to replace damaged water supplies, sign agreements with surface owners (with arbitration if they can't agree), restore the land after drilling, and post bonds to pay for cleanup. It also would have created a federal program to plug and clean up abandoned wells.
analysis.who_benefits: Ranchers, farmers, and rural homeowners in Western states who own the surface of land where the federal government owns the minerals underneath. They would gain the right to negotiate with drillers, get paid for crop and property damage, have contaminated water replaced, and see land restored after drilling. States and tribes would get federal help cleaning up abandoned wells.

how_it_helps.text: Operators would have to replace the water supply of any user whose domestic or agricultural water is contaminated, diminished, or cut off by drilling operations, and submit water management plans with lease applications.

Before drilling on split-estate land, operators would have to reach a written surface-use agreement with the landowner, with operator-paid arbitration if they can't agree, covering compensation for lost income, damaged crops, forage, and livestock, and site reclamation.

Operators would have to meet reclamation standards restoring the land to its prior uses and post bonds sufficient to complete reclamation, with surface owners able to participate in bond-setting and release decisions.

The Interior Department would run a program to remediate abandoned wells on federal lands and drill sites for federally owned minerals, with $5 million a year authorized for fiscal 2008 and 2009, plus technical assistance for states and tribes on abandoned wells elsewhere.

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas operators drilling on federal leases would bear the costs: replacing damaged water supplies, compensating landowners, paying arbitration and attorney fees, posting reclamation bonds, and cleaning up abandoned wells. These costs would likely be passed into production economics; some marginal drilling on split-estate lands might not go forward.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal leases

drawbacks.text: Requiring agreements, bonds, and reclamation would raise drilling costs and could delay or cancel some projects, which the bill's own findings acknowledge as a tension with domestic energy production — the bill explicitly frames itself as balancing development with protection rather than stopping it.

The arbitration process and a Secretary's discretion to authorize drilling without an agreement (if the operator shows a good-faith attempt and posts a bond) still allow drilling over a landowner's objection, just with compensation attached.
The abandoned-well programs are authorized at only $5 million a year and rely on 'maximum extent feasible' cost recovery from responsible parties, so the scale of cleanup they could fund is limited.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For landowners and water users, the benefits are direct and concrete: enforceable water replacement, a seat at the table with drillers, and bonds that guarantee cleanup. The costs fall on operators, and the bill preserves their right of access to the minerals — even without a landowner's agreement — so it constrains but does not block development. Its main design weakness is modest funding for abandoned-well cleanup.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Natural Resources Committee and then to its Energy and Mineral Resources Subcommittee, which never acted on it, and it died there when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.

narrative.text: Representative Mark Udall of Colorado introduced the bill on February 16, 2007, and it was referred to the House Committee on Natural Resources.
On March 2, 2007, it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources, where it stayed for the rest of the Congress.
The bill had no cosponsors and received no committee markup, no floor vote, and no Senate counterpart action before the Congress ended.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas operators drilling on federal split-estate lands are better off: none of the water-replacement, surface-owner agreement, bonding, or reclamation requirements ever took effect, and drilling continued under the looser pre-existing rules.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers on federal leases

against.what_they_did: Received the referral on February 16, 2007 and never held a markup or advanced the bill.

against.name: Subcommittee on Energy and Mineral Resources
against.what_they_did: Received the referral on March 2, 2007 and took no action on the bill for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: No votes were ever taken and the bill had zero cosponsors, so the partisan shape of support or opposition never showed itself in the record.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers on federal leases (including coalbed methane)
industries.note: The bill would have imposed water-replacement duties, surface-owner agreements and compensation, reclamation bonds, and abandoned-well cleanup costs on federal-lease operators. These are real compliance costs, though the bill still guaranteed operators access to the minerals.

industries.industry: Western farmers and ranchers holding split-estate surface land
industries.note: Surface owners would gain negotiation rights, compensation for damages, water replacement, and bonding-backed reclamation. This is a landowner group rather than an industry, but it is the concentrated beneficiary of the bill.
